conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: FailedSwingLowBreakoutLong
candidates.quote: Similarly, the first failed breakout below a prior swing low is a lower low buy setup. Place an order to buy at one tick above the high of the prior bar on a stop.
candidates.description: The current bar breaks below the lowest low of the prior N bars but closes back clearly above that broken level (a failed downside breakout) - a with-trend or countertrend buy signal, the mirror of a failed higher-high short.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] < lowest(low, n)[1] && close[0] > lowest(low, n)[1] + toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the high of the prior bar, trailed down bar by bar until filled or momentum gets too strong to keep shorting/buying against

complexity.reason: a window-loop lowest(low,n) plus a fixed-offset close comparison

notes: Brooks's actual order management (trail the stop-entry order up/down bar by bar while unfilled) is simplified to a single signal-bar test per the close-and-next-open convention.
n is a reading of 'prior swing low'; Brooks gives no explicit bar count here.

candidates.name: FailureToMakeNewExtremeStrongTrend
candidates.quote: Failure to fall below the low of the prior bar in a strong bull trend or to rally above the high of the prior bar in a strong bear trend. This indicates urgency and a strong trend.
candidates.description: The current bar fails to trade below the low of the prior bar (bull case) - a sign of urgency and trend strength, used as a with-trend filter gating other bull entries.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: single fixed-offset comparison of low[0] to low[1]

notes: Meant to be ANDed with a separate strong-bull-trend context primitive defined elsewhere; not useful alone.

candidates.name: FailedPullbackToMovingAverage
candidates.quote: Failure of a pullback to reach the moving average. This indicates urgency and a strong trend.
candidates.description: In a bull trend, the current pullback bar's low stays above the moving average without touching it - a sign of a strong trend, used as a with-trend entry filter.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (context filter, not itself an order)

complexity.reason: needs the 20-bar EMA (moving average) primitive maintained bar to bar

notes: movingAverage is the standard 20-bar EMA primitive defined in earlier chapters; not redefined here.

candidates.name: OutsideBarBreakoutAvoidFilter
candidates.quote: Outside bars are basically one-bar trading ranges, and most trading range breakout entries fail. You should only rarely enter on a breakout of an outside bar because the risk is too great.
candidates.description: Primitive: the prior bar is an outside bar (its range engulfs the bar before it). Applied NEGATED ahead of any breakout-style entry to block stop entries beyond either extreme of a just-completed outside bar.

complexity.reason: two fixed-offset comparisons, no window loop

notes: Negate this condition (per-placement negate toggle) to gate other breakout entries, the same pattern as TimeWindow's negated use in EEC #18.

candidates.name: TwoBarReversalEntryAfterLargeBar
candidates.quote: Since this was a two-bar reversal, the safest entry was below the lower of the two bars, which was the large bull trend bar, because very often the market goes below the bear bar, but not below both bars.
candidates.description: After a two-bar reversal (a small bar closing opposite a larger trend bar that preceded it), the safer stop-entry is beyond the extreme of the pair rather than only beyond the current bar - long version: enter above the higher high of the two bars.
candidates.pseudocode: close[1] < open[1] && (open[1] - close[1]) >= priorBarDominance * (close[0] - open[0]) && entryLevel = max(high[0], high[1])
candidates.book_order_type: buy/sell stop one tick beyond the extreme of the two-bar pair, not just the current bar

complexity.reason: cross-bar state over a fixed two-bar window, no swing-pivot detection needed

notes: Brooks gives no numeric test for 'large' vs 'small' bar in the pair; priorBarDominance is a reading of it.

candidates.name: FailedProfitTargetReversalExit
candidates.quote: If the order is not filled by the time the bar closes... a move that goes only five ticks and then reverses often indicates that the trend traders have lost control and a pullback or reversal is imminent.
candidates.description: Generalizes the chapter's 5-, 9-, and 17-tick 'failed scalp' examples: once open profit has come within toleranceDollars of a fixed profit target and the market then closes beyond the low of the prior bar, exit rather than wait for the limit order to fill.
candidates.book_order_type: originally a limit order profit target that goes unfilled; exit instead at the market/on a stop once the prior bar's extreme is broken

complexity.reason: reads position-history (peak open profit) plus a fixed-offset price comparison

notes: Distinct from ProfitProtector/ProfitProtectorRatio: the trigger here is a price-structure break (close below the prior bar's low), not a retracement fraction of peak profit.
toleranceDollars defaults to one Emini tick's dollar value ($12.50); targetDollars is illustrative, Brooks uses many different targets (4-tick, 2-point, 4-point scalps).

candidates.name: BreakoutPullbackRetestHoldContinuation
candidates.quote: If there is a bar that turns up at two ticks above the high of the signal bar, then it missed the breakeven stops by a tick. The market failed to flush the bulls out. Traders will then buy above this breakout test bar.
candidates.description: Price pulls back to retest a prior breakout level (a recent swing high, for a long continuation) but stays within toleranceTicks above it instead of closing back below - a with-trend breakout-pullback continuation buy.
candidates.pseudocode: low[0] >= recentSwingHigh - toleranceTicks * tickSize && close[0] > open[0]
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the breakout-test bar's high

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection to identify the breakout level being retested

notes: recentSwingHigh is the swing-high/breakout-pullback primitive defined in earlier chapters; not redefined here.

candidates.name: BuyBearSpikeInEstablishedBullTrend
candidates.quote: Instead of looking for shorts, experienced traders will often buy on the close of that spike down or on the open of the next day... They know that most attempts to reverse fail and the first attempt almost always is followed by a new high.
candidates.description: In an established bull trend, a sharp bear spike down toward or through the moving average / trend line is usually a failed reversal attempt; buy on the close of the spike bar (or the open of the next bar) instead of waiting for more confirmation.
candidates.pseudocode: bullTrendContext && (close[1] - close[0]) >= spikeFraction * close[1] && close[0] <= movingAverage[0] + toleranceTicks * tickSize
candidates.book_order_type: buy at the close of the spike bar or the open of the following bar; also mentioned as buying calls to cap overnight risk

complexity.reason: combines a trend-context judgment, a magnitude-of-decline threshold, and proximity to the moving average / trend line

notes: Illustrated with AAPL (8% earnings gap) and NTAP (16% sell-off) on daily charts, and SPY on a 60-minute chart; Brooks gives no numeric spike threshold, spikeFraction is a reading.
The options-based version of this trade (buying calls at the spike bottom) is out of scope - see rejected.

candidates.name: MagnetFailureRetestSetup
candidates.quote: Failure to reach a magnet, like a measured move target, a prior swing high or low, a trend line, or a trend channel line. This often leads to a pullback and then another attempt to reach the magnet.
candidates.description: When price comes close to but fails to reach a magnet (measured-move target, prior swing extreme, or trend line) and pulls back, expect a renewed push back toward that magnet; trade the pullback in the direction of the original move.
candidates.pseudocode: // needs a design decision on how 'magnet' targets (measured moves, swing extremes, trend/channel lines) are represented before a concrete test can be written
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (setup concept, not a specific order)

complexity.reason: the concept is real but requires deciding how to represent measured-move / trend-line 'magnets' before any bar-level test can be coded

notes: Ties together several already-hard primitives (measured moves, trend lines) around a single failure/retest idea.

candidates.name: HeadAndShouldersPriorStrengthFilter
candidates.quote: The shape alone is not enough reason to place a countertrend trade. You always want to see some earlier countertrend strength prior to the reversal pattern.
candidates.description: A head-and-shoulders (or similar) reversal pattern is not tradeable on shape alone; require evidence of prior countertrend strength (e.g. an already-broken trend line, or a prior strong opposite-direction leg) before taking the pattern's signal.
candidates.pseudocode: // 'prior countertrend strength' is undefined at the bar level until a specific test (e.g. a trend-line break, or a same-direction momentum bar) is chosen

complexity.reason: the qualifying 'earlier countertrend strength' is left undefined by Brooks; a design decision is needed on what counts

candidates.name: TrendVsRangeBreakoutContext
candidates.quote: Most breakout attempts fail, especially when the market is in a trading range... In a strong trend, they do the opposite... traders instead will buy on a stop above the top of the range, since they expect another leg up.
candidates.description: Whether to fade a range breakout or follow a trend breakout depends on classifying the session as a trading-range day or a trend day; fade breakouts when ranging, follow them when trending.
candidates.pseudocode: // 'is the session a trading range or a trend' is the research-grade classification named directly in the mining brief

complexity.reason: trading-range-vs-trend-day classification needs a design decision before it can be coded, as flagged in the mining brief

candidates.name: FailedReversalPatternContinuation
candidates.quote: Failed final flag (the reversal attempt fails and sets up a breakout pullback). Failed wedge... Failed reversal, like a failed double bottom or top or a failed head and shoulders pattern.
candidates.description: General statement covering several named reversal patterns (final flag, wedge, double top/bottom, head-and-shoulders): when one of these fails to reverse the trend, it typically produces a breakout-pullback continuation entry in the original trend direction shortly afterward.
candidates.pseudocode: // composes a named reversal-pattern primitive (final flag / wedge / double top-bottom / head-and-shoulders, defined in other chapters) with a subsequent breakout-pullback continuation test
candidates.book_order_type: buy/sell stop beyond the breakout-pullback bar that follows the failed pattern

complexity.reason: depends on variable-length pattern recognition (final flag, wedge, double top/bottom, H&S) defined elsewhere, plus a breakout-pullback continuation test

notes: An umbrella statement rather than a single mechanizable test; the authoring pass should wire it to whichever pattern primitives already exist per chapter (04-08).

rejected.quote: if the market goes 16 ticks above the signal bar high, it has about an 80 percent chance of reaching 17 or 18 ticks
rejected.reason: an empirical probability aside about continuation odds, not a bar-level if-then condition

rejected.quote: A one-tick failed breakout on the 5 minute chart... is often also a one-tick failed breakout on a higher time frame, like a 15 or 60 minute chart
rejected.reason: requires simultaneously evaluating two bar timeframes (5-minute and 60-minute) against each other, which the engine does not model as one signal

rejected.quote: Every stock has distinct characteristics in its trading, presumably because many of the same people trade it every day
rejected.reason: requires knowledge of trader identity/composition, data the engine cannot have

rejected.quote: The bear trend bar was probably based on some scary news report
rejected.reason: requires news data, not available to the engine

chapter_summary: Chapter 9 argues that roughly 40 percent of good-looking setups fail, and that failures usually trap traders whose forced exits fuel a tradeable move in the opposite direction (or, in a strong trend, a with-trend continuation). Most of the chapter is worked chart examples (Figures 9.1-9.19) reapplying primitives already mined in Chapters 2-8 (signal bars, double tops/bottoms, wedges, high2/low2, outside/inside bars) to failure scenarios rather than introducing new pattern shapes. The genuinely new material mined here is: failed swing-high/low breakouts as reversal entries, a family of N-tick 'failed scalp' profit-target exits, several strong-trend context filters (failure to make a new extreme, failure of a pullback to reach the moving average), an outside-bar breakout-avoidance filter with a safer two-bar-reversal entry, and three research-grade ideas (magnet failure/retest, required prior countertrend strength before a reversal pattern, and trading-range-vs-trend-day classification) that need design decisions before they can be coded.
